# Graph `example_graph`

## When to use

Use it for questions about which item is stored where and for changes to that.

## Is it available here?

Run `graph graphs --json`. Use this skill only if an item named `example_graph` is listed (title: Example graph). Pass `--graph example_graph` to every command, as the examples here do, so they work in every directory; a project whose pointer makes `example_graph` the default may leave it out.

Before your first `graph` command, load the `graph-cli` skill as well: it explains the commands, the output envelope and safe writes. This skill says what the graph holds. Two of its ground rules apply from the first call:

- Run each call as a plain command that starts with `graph`: no `cd`, variables, loops, pipes or heredocs, which a restricted harness refuses. If a call is refused, run it again in that form before you give up.
- For a few fields, a count or a join, use `graph query` and `RETURN` only those columns (`graph describe schema --compact --json` lists the patterns), or `--fields <attr>,<attr>` on `find`, `get` and `neighbors`, instead of filtering JSON with another program.

## Subject areas

| Module | Prefix | What it holds | Types | Actions | Links to other modules |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `inventory` | `inv` | Physical items, where they are stored and how they are grouped. | 3 | 2 | none |

Built-in modules, shared by every graph: `core`.

- Before you work in a module, read it: `graph describe module <module> --graph example_graph` lists its types, its relations, its links to and from other modules (with the other module named) and its rules. Read its text; `--json` is more than twice the size.
- To find a term whose module you do not know: `graph describe search <text> --graph example_graph --json` (types, relations, fields, enum values and states).
- For the fields, states and relations of one type: `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json`.

## Changes

2 named actions; for a change use one before you write with the primitives. Dry run first: `graph do <action> --param <name>=<value> --graph example_graph --dry-run`, read what it will change, then run it without `--dry-run`.

- `move_item(item: ref inv:Item, location: ref inv:Location)`: Store an item in another location.

More: `graph describe actions --module <module> --graph example_graph`; find one: `graph describe search <text> --kind action --graph example_graph --json`; preconditions and use: `graph describe action <action> --graph example_graph`. For an entity you already have, `graph get <id> --affordances --graph example_graph` lists the actions that fit it, whether each applies and what blocks it.

## Names and ids

- Aliases: `inv:Category` `CAT-0001`, `inv:Item` `ITEM-0001`, `inv:Location` `LOC-0001`. The number is zero-padded to 4 digits (`CAT-0001`, never `CAT-1`) and grows past 9999. A full id works everywhere; on the command line 8 or more trailing hex digits of it work too.
- No type of this graph has names (label roles), so `graph lookup` finds nothing; use `graph find --graph example_graph`.
- `graph search <value> --graph example_graph --json` searches names and every text field, forgiving case, accents, typos and parts of words. Its results are suggestions: read one with `graph get` before you use it.

## Model

Every type with all its fields, lifecycles, relations and rules: [references/model.md](references/model.md). The live source, which wins when they differ: `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json`.
